title: lemo-animi: Open-source stop-motion plugin turns one sentence into a 40-second film
summary: Want to make stop-motion without posing every frame by hand? This open-source plugin lets Codex or Claude Code start from one sentence and handle the script, images, frame sequencing, sound, and review automatically — defaulting to 40-second films.
ai_summary: lemo-animi is an open-source stop-motion skill that installs into Codex or Claude Code and turns one sentence into a short film. It ships with 8 material styles; each demo film is generated from a single sentence. During production the agent writes the story and shot list, uses an image model to create characters, backgrounds, and an 8-pose action sheet, then sequences frames on twos or on threes, adds a score built from real instrument samples plus foley, and finally opens a local review console for shot-by-shot changes. Default output is 40 seconds, 24 fps, 1920×1080; longer films generate more images. Personal use is free; commercial use requires a license. Main limits: the first run downloads about 1.7 GB of environment, only macOS or Linux is supported, and Claude Code mode relies on the local Codex for image generation by default.
brief: Turn one sentence into a stop-motion short film, 40 seconds by default, with 8 built-in material styles.
The agent writes the script, generates images, sequences frames on twos or threes, and adds score and foley.
First use downloads about 1.7 GB (about 300 MB Python environment + about 1.4 GB instrument samples).
Free for personal non-commercial use (CC BY-NC 4.0); commercial use requires a license. Narration uses Microsoft Edge online voices.

blocks.p: lemo-animi is Lemomo's newly released open-source stop-motion skill — effectively a filmmaking plugin for the AI coding assistants Codex and Claude Code. Give it one sentence, such as “Make a 40-second clay stop-motion film about a little penguin learning to make pancakes,” and the agent writes the story and shot list, generates characters and sets, animates them frame by frame, adds music and sound effects, and hands you a finished film.

Stop-motion is handmade animation: pose an object, shoot a frame, move it slightly, shoot another, and playback makes it move. Its stepped rhythm is the point, not a bug. lemo-animi moves this process into code: an image model draws characters, backgrounds, and action sheets, while Python cuts the action sheets into frames, times them, and adds camera movement, light, and color.

What comes out is a complete film, with opening and closing titles, score, foley, and optional narration and subtitles. The default output is 1920×1080; you can also choose vertical 1080×1920 or square 1080×1080, at 24 frames per second.

sections.h: The 8 materials and what each can make

blocks.p: The author gives each material a fixed style pack — prompt template, lighting, camera language, score, and foley are all matched. You can select a style by Chinese name, English name, or id. All 8 demo films were generated by the skill itself from a single sentence.

rows: The Little Light on a Snowy Night

blocks.p: The demo stories all have a small twist: in the clay film, the little penguin flips a pancake, fails twice, and succeeds on the third try; in the cardboard film, the “moon landing” is really a bedroom-floor fantasy, with an ending card that reads “Actual flight distance: 30 cm.” Those details also come from the agent's script.

sections.h: What happens between the sentence and the finished film?

blocks.p: After the environment is installed, the agent asks all the questions at once — style, runtime, aspect ratio, narration, opening and closing titles — with defaults listed first; you can also simply reply “all defaults.” It then works through to the finished film, sending only short progress updates along the way.

fig.title: From one sentence to final cut: plan, generate images, sequence frames, score, review
fig.subtitle: Schematic: the agent connects the stages automatically; the names here are simplified.

steps.name: Plan
steps.desc: Story outline, per-section timings, beats, shot list, image-generation list

steps.name: Generate images
steps.desc: Character designs, backgrounds, 8-pose action sheet, 2×2 close-up sheet, transparent backgrounds

steps.name: Sequence frames
steps.desc: Cut the action sheet into individual frames, run on twos or threes, add camera movement, contact shadows, light, and color

steps.name: Add sound
steps.desc: Original score, foley for every contact, optional narration and subtitles

steps.name: Review
steps.desc: The agent reviews and revises once on its own, then opens the review console for you.

blocks.p: The crucial step is frame sequencing. The image model doesn't animate; it only produces static action sheets. Making characters move comes from Python cutting the sheets apart and repeating each pose to the beat.

fig.title: The same action on twos takes one fewer frame than on threes
fig.subtitle: Schematic: amber frames are the frames where the same pose is repeated.

rows.v: Each action sheet image stays for 2 frames
Each action sheet image stays for 3 frames

blocks.p: “On twos” means each action sheet image holds for 2 frames on the timeline; “on threes” holds for 3 frames. Higher hold counts save images but feel choppier — and that is where much of stop-motion's stepped character comes from.

fig.text: Stop-motion was always shot one frame at a time. The stepped rhythm is the point.

sections.h: How many images does a longer film need?

blocks.p: Most of the cost goes to image generation. The author lists shot and image counts by runtime: longer films mean more shots and more generated images.

fig.title: Longer films mean more shots and more generated images
fig.subtitle: Highlighted is the default 40-second tier; image counts are approximate.

blocks.p: If you want a richer plot, ask for a specific storyline up front; for a quick test, the 20-second tier saves image generations. If you want everything drawn in code with no image model, the author also has lemo-opuscar, which offers 99 film styles built entirely in code.

sections.h: How to install? Codex or Claude Code?

blocks.p: Before installing, you need macOS or Linux, ffmpeg (on macOS: `brew install ffmpeg`), and Python 3.11–3.13 or uv. The first time you make a film, the agent automatically checks and installs the environment: starting from scratch downloads about 1.7 GB — roughly 300 MB for the Python runtime and roughly 1.4 GB for the instrument samples used in the score, with resumable downloads. Everything goes in ~/lemo-animi-env.

For Codex, run these two commands in the terminal or app: `codex plugin marketplace add lemomo-ai/lemo-animi`, then `codex plugin add lemo-animi@lemomo-ai`; after installing, start a new conversation. For Claude Code, enter `/plugin install lemo-animi --marketplace lemomo-ai/lemo-animi` in the conversation, then run `/reload-plugins` or start a new session.

blocks.p: For Codex, the author recommends GPT-6.2 Sol or GPT-6.2 Astra with reasoning High; GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra at High or above also work. Claude Code must use auto mode, because one film can run hundreds of commands — the default mode asks before each one.

sections.h: Review console: not satisfied? Change it frame by frame

blocks.p: A film isn't finished the first time it renders. After the film is assembled, the agent opens the review console in your local browser: the film on top, clips arranged by shot below, and notes on the right. Using it takes four steps:

list: Stop at the moment you want to change: Space plays/pauses, and the arrow keys step one frame at a time.
Press Enter to write the issue: the timecode, frame number, and shot are captured automatically, and a pin is placed on the clip.
Click “Submit to agent”: it revises the items one by one, replies under each note with what changed, and logs a new version.
When you're satisfied, click “Approve”: the agent delivers the film.

blocks.p: After the review console opens, the agent waits at most 30 minutes. Nothing is lost if you go over: notes are saved to the film folder as you write. When you finish, click “Submit to agent” or “Approve,” then return to the conversation and say “I'm done reviewing.” If the review console opened as a local file, click “Copy notes” and paste them into the conversation.

sections.h: Pricing and licensing: free for personal use, commercial use requires a license

blocks.p: Personal use is always free. The license is CC BY-NC 4.0: free for non-commercial use as long as you credit “lemo-animi by Lemomo (LemoLab).” Any commercial use — ads, client work, monetized channels, products — requires a commercial license; the contact email is in the repository.
Narration uses Microsoft Edge online voices by default and can be replaced; narration text is sent to Microsoft's speech service. If you're sensitive about data uploads, keep that in mind.

list: Commercial license pricing: the post only gives a contact email, no price.
Windows support: the post only lists macOS or Linux.
Image generation costs: images come from a model, but the post doesn't list per-image or per-film generation fees.
Timing for the in-test shadow puppetry, flat papercut, clay relief, and miniature model styles: the post only says “in a future version.”
Comparison with other AI animation tools: the post gives no named competitors or benchmarks.

blocks.p: The value is clear: people who can't draw, pose frames, or edit can get a stop-motion short with full narrative, score, and sound effects from a single sentence. It removes the barrier of learning animation from scratch, and it suits content creators, teachers, brand clips, or anyone who just wants to play.

The tradeoffs are just as clear: the first run downloads about 1.7 GB of environment; it only runs on macOS/Linux; commercial use costs extra; and the Claude Code path still defaults to local Codex for image generation. Also, this is the first version, and the author encourages everyone to open issues.

If you already use Codex and want fast output, this is the low-friction path. If you only have Claude Code and no Codex, it still works, but you'll need to configure an image model yourself. If you plan to take client work or run a commercial channel, contact the author about a license first.

callout.title: One-line takeaway
callout.text: One sentence → a stop-motion short; free for personal use, licensed for commercial work.
